_meta.description: OSCE Radiology Guide — static data for the guide page (quick reference, pattern index, exam technique). Case content is AI-generated and stored in DB.

quickRules.meaning: SB < 3cm, LB < 6cm, Caecum < 9cm. Above = dilated.
Valvulae conniventes, short fluid levels
Haustra, long fluid levels
Perforation until proven otherwise — surgical emergency
But only 10% gallstones visible on AXR

items: Small bowel: central location, valvulae conniventes (folds cross full width), < 3cm diameter. Normal: no more than 2-3 air-fluid levels.
Large bowel: peripheral location, haustra (folds cross part-way), < 6cm diameter (caecum < 9cm). Remember the 3-6-9 rule.
SBO vs LBO: SB = many central dilated loops with short fluid levels. LB = few peripheral dilated loops with long fluid levels.
Rectum: gas normally present. Absent rectal gas in obstruction.
Faecal loading: mottled grey appearance, distribution pattern.
steps.label: Intraluminal Gas (Bowel Gas Pattern)

items: Erect CXR: air under diaphragm (most sensitive test for pneumoperitoneum).
Supine AXR: Rigler sign (both sides of bowel wall outlined by air), falciform ligament sign, football sign (large oval lucency).
Causes: perforated viscus (peptic ulcer, diverticulitis, appendicitis) — surgical emergency.
Pitfall: recent surgery or laparoscopy can cause benign free air for up to 7 days.
steps.label: Extraluminal Gas (FREE AIR = EMERGENCY)

items: Renal tract: kidney stones (90% radio-opaque), staghorn calculi, ureteric stones, bladder stones.
Biliary: gallstones (only 10% radio-opaque — most are radiolucent), porcelain gallbladder.
Vascular: aortic calcification (AAA if > 3cm), iliac artery calcification.
Other: pancreatic (chronic pancreatitis), appendicolith, phleboliths (round, in pelvis — benign).
steps.label: Calcifications

items: Liver: size (should not extend below right costal margin), density.
Spleen: visible? Enlarged? (tip below left costal margin).
Kidneys: both visible? Normal size (3-3.5 vertebral bodies). Psoas lines intact (loss = retroperitoneal pathology).
Bladder: distended? Displaced?
Fat lines: properitoneal fat stripe, psoas margins (obliteration = fluid/inflammation).
steps.label: Solid Organs & Soft Tissues

items: Spine: alignment, vertebral body height, disc spaces, pedicles (absent = metastasis).
Pelvis: sacroiliac joints, pubic symphysis, hip joints.
Lower ribs: fractures (especially left lower ribs → splenic injury).
steps.label: Bones

items: Lines/tubes: NG tube tip position (should be beyond GOJ), urinary catheter, surgical drains.
Foreign bodies: ingested objects, retained surgical instruments.
External artefacts: buttons, jewellery, clothing — don't mistake for pathology.
steps.label: Artefacts & Foreign Bodies

axr.title: Abdominal X-Ray: Systematic Approach
axr.views: AP supine (standard). Erect AXR for air-fluid levels. Erect CXR for free air under diaphragm.

quickRules.meaning: Acute blood is hyperdense on non-contrast CT
Arterial (MMA), lucid interval
quickRules.rule: EDH = biconvex, does NOT cross sutures

quickRules.meaning: Venous (bridging veins), elderly/anticoagulated
Clinically significant. > 10mm + falling GCS = surgical emergency
Earliest sign of raised ICP — before ventricle changes
Hydrocephalus (not atrophy — atrophy has prominent sulci)

items: Acute blood = hyperdense (white, 50-70 HU) on non-contrast CT. No contrast needed to see it.
Extra-axial: EDH (biconvex, does NOT cross sutures), SDH (crescent, DOES cross sutures), SAH (blood in sulci, cisterns, Sylvian fissures).
Intraparenchymal haemorrhage: location (basal ganglia = hypertensive, lobar = amyloid/tumour).
Intraventricular blood: blood layering in ventricles.
Pitfall: do NOT confuse choroid plexus calcifications (normal, bright white in ventricles) with blood.
steps.label: Blood

items: Quadrigeminal cistern: 'smile sign' — should be open. Effacement = raised ICP / early herniation.
Suprasellar cistern: star-shaped. Asymmetry or effacement = mass effect.
Basal cisterns (ambient, prepontine): blood here = SAH. Effacement = raised ICP.
Cistern effacement is often the EARLIEST sign of raised ICP — look before ventricles change.
steps.label: Cisterns

items: Grey-white matter differentiation: loss = cerebral oedema or early ischaemia. White matter is darker (more fat/myelin).
Symmetry: compare both hemispheres. Asymmetry = focal pathology.
Midline shift: > 5mm is clinically significant. > 10mm with decreasing GCS = surgical emergency.
Sulci: effaced (oedema/raised ICP) or prominent (atrophy).
Focal hypo/hyperdensities: hypodense = oedema/infarct, hyperdense = blood/calcification.
steps.label: Brain Parenchyma

items: Size: symmetric? Dilated = hydrocephalus or atrophy.
Hydrocephalus vs Atrophy: dilated ventricles + effaced sulci = hydrocephalus. Dilated ventricles + prominent sulci = atrophy.
Temporal horns: dilatation is an early sign of raised ICP (normally slit-like).
Slit-like ventricles: suggests diffuse cerebral oedema.
Blood in ventricles: layering posteriorly in occipital horns.
steps.label: Ventricles

items: Skull vault: linear fractures (distinguish from suture lines — check contralateral side for symmetry).
Base of skull fractures: look for fluid in mastoid air cells or sphenoid sinus.
Facial bones: orbital walls, zygomatic arch.
Sinuses: air-fluid levels in trauma = fracture until proven otherwise.
steps.label: Bone (use bone windows)

ct_brain.title: CT Brain: Systematic Approach
ct_brain.views: Axial non-contrast (standard for acute). Bone windows for fractures. Soft tissue windows for parenchyma. CTA if vascular pathology suspected.

quickRules.meaning: Consolidation, effusion, mass, collapse, foreign body
Pneumothorax, hyperinflation, emphysema, cavitation
Cardiomegaly, widened mediastinum, hilar enlargement, mass
Tracheal deviation, mediastinal shift, elevated diaphragm, herniation
Normal heart size. AP magnifies — cannot assess CTR on AP film
Always check outer 1cm of lung fields — where pneumothorax and small nodules hide
List ALL findings before analysing any one. Don't stop at the first abnormality.

items: Trachea: midline? Deviation AWAY from = tension pneumothorax, large effusion. Deviation TOWARDS = collapse, volume loss.
Carina: visible at T4-T5? Splayed > 100 degrees = left atrial enlargement or subcarinal mass.
Main bronchi: patent? Right main bronchus is more vertical — foreign bodies favour the right side.
If intubated: ETT tip should be 2-4 cm above carina.
steps.label: Airway

items: Lung fields: compare side to side — should be equally translucent. One side whiter = consolidation/effusion/collapse. One side blacker = pneumothorax/hyperinflation.
Costophrenic angles: sharp = normal. Blunted = effusion (>175-200ml needed to blunt). Meniscus sign = fluid.
Pleural line: visible line with NO lung markings beyond it = pneumothorax. Deep sulcus sign on supine film.
Lung markings: should extend to periphery. Absent peripherally = pneumothorax. Prominent/upper lobe diversion = pulmonary oedema.
Consolidation: dense white opacity. Air bronchograms (dark branching lines within white area) = alveolar filling.
steps.label: Breathing (Lungs & Pleura)

items: Heart size: CTR < 0.5 on PA = normal. CTR > 0.5 = cardiomegaly. WARNING: AP film magnifies heart — cannot assess CTR reliably on AP.
Heart shape: boot-shaped = RV hypertrophy. Globular = pericardial effusion. Normal silhouette: right atrium, left ventricle borders visible.
Mediastinum: width < 8cm on PA. Widened = aortic dissection, lymphadenopathy, mass. URGENT if widened + chest pain.
Hila: left hilum normally slightly higher than right. Bilateral hilar enlargement = sarcoidosis, lymphoma. Unilateral = tumour.
Aortic knob: visible? Unfolded/calcified = atherosclerosis. Absent/obscured = dissection.
steps.label: Circulation (Heart & Mediastinum)

items: Ribs: trace each one — fractures (especially posterior, easy to miss). Flail segment = 3+ consecutive rib fractures. Rib notching = coarctation of aorta.
Clavicles: fractures, AC joint separation.
Spine: vertebral body height, alignment, compression fractures.
Soft tissues: surgical emphysema (air in soft tissues = lucent streaks in neck/chest wall). Mastectomy (absent breast shadow — explains asymmetric density).
steps.label: Disability (Bones & Soft Tissue)

items: IMPORTANT: Complete your ENTIRE ABCDE scan before analysing any finding. The temptation is to stop at the first abnormality — resist it. List everything, then interpret.
PERIPHERAL 1CM: Always check the outer 1cm of each lung field — pneumothorax, small nodules, and effusion margins hide here.
APICES: Pancoast tumour (apical mass + rib erosion), TB (upper lobe cavitation), pneumothorax (air rises).
BEHIND HEART: left lower lobe collapse/consolidation hides behind cardiac silhouette — look for loss of left hemidiaphragm.
BELOW DIAPHRAGM: free air (pneumoperitoneum) = crescent of black under right hemidiaphragm on erect film. Gastric bubble normally under left.
DIAPHRAGM: right normally 1-2 cm higher than left. Flattened = hyperinflation/COPD. Elevated = phrenic nerve palsy, hepatomegaly.
Lines/tubes: ETT (2-4 cm above carina), CVC (tip in SVC), NG tube (tip below diaphragm), chest drain (in pleural space).
Adequacy: Rotation (medial clavicle ends equidistant from spinous process), Inspiration (5-7 anterior ribs above diaphragm), Exposure (just see vertebrae through cardiac shadow).
steps.label: Everything Else (Review Areas)

cxr.title: Chest X-Ray: ABCDE Approach
cxr.views: PA erect (standard — accurate CTR, sharp CP angles). AP (portable/sick — magnifies heart, widens mediastinum). Lateral (retrosternal space, posterior pathology).

quickRules.meaning: Fractures hide on single views — AP + Lateral minimum
ALWAYS abnormal = assume occult fracture
Fat-fluid level on lateral = intra-articular fracture
Should bisect middle third of capitellum — if not = supracondylar fracture
2nd MT base aligns with middle cuneiform — malalignment = commonly missed injury
Flattened = calcaneal fracture (normal 20-40°)

items: Joint congruency: are the articular surfaces parallel and properly aligned? Any step-off = fracture or dislocation.
Dislocation: is the bone completely out of joint? (Shoulder: humeral head vs glenoid. Elbow: olecranon vs trochlea. Knee: tibia vs femur.)
Subluxation: partial displacement — bone still partially in contact with joint surface.
Joint-specific lines: Anterior humeral line should pass through middle third of capitellum (elbow). Radiocapitellar line should point to capitellum in all views.
Lisfranc alignment (foot): medial border of 2nd metatarsal base should align with medial border of middle cuneiform. Malalignment = Lisfranc injury (commonly missed).
steps.label: Alignment

items: Trace EVERY cortex systematically — cortical break = fracture. Follow the outer edge of every bone like drawing an outline.
Subtle fractures: look for cortical buckling, angulation, or a faint lucent line. Compare with the other side if in doubt.
Density: focal lucency = lytic lesion (tumour, infection). Focal sclerosis = healing fracture, bone island, or sclerotic metastasis.
Periosteal reaction: new bone along the shaft = fracture healing, infection, or tumour. Sunburst/onion-skin = aggressive (sarcoma).
Joint-specific: Tibial plateau depression (knee — look on lateral). Bankart lesion (shoulder — inferior glenoid). Bohler angle < 20 degrees (calcaneus — flattened = fracture).
steps.label: Bones

items: Joint space: should be uniform. Asymmetric narrowing = OA (weight-bearing side). Diffuse narrowing = inflammatory (RA).
Effusion: Knee — suprapatellar pouch fullness on lateral view. Lipohaemarthrosis (fat-fluid level) = intra-articular fracture.
Fat pads (ELBOW): posterior fat pad visible = ALWAYS abnormal = occult fracture. Anterior 'sail sign' = raised anterior fat pad = effusion.
Osteophytes: bony spurs at joint margins = OA. Subchondral sclerosis + cysts also = OA.
Erosions: marginal erosions = RA. Periarticular osteopenia + symmetric joint involvement = inflammatory arthritis.
steps.label: Cartilage & Joints

items: Swelling: focal soft tissue swelling points to the injury site — look at the underlying bone carefully.
Fat pad displacement: elbow posterior fat pad (see above). Knee suprapatellar fat pad.
Calcification: supraspinatus tendon (shoulder — calcific tendinitis). Meniscal calcification (knee — chondrocalcinosis). Achilles tendon.
Foreign bodies: glass IS visible on X-ray (radio-opaque). Wood is NOT visible. Metal is bright white.
Muscle planes: loss of normal fat planes between muscles = deep soft tissue injury or haematoma.
steps.label: Soft Tissues

msk.subtitle: Applies to: Knee, Shoulder, Elbow, Foot
msk.title: MSK X-Ray: ABCS Approach
msk.views: MINIMUM 2 views at 90 degrees (AP + Lateral) — fractures hide on single views. Special views: Skyline/sunrise (patella), Axillary/Y-view (shoulder — essential for posterior dislocation), Oblique (foot — 5th MT base), Scaphoid views (wrist).

air.label: Air / Lucency
air.description: Black on X-ray, black on CT. Air where it should not be.

fluid.label: Fluid / White-out
fluid.description: White on X-ray (meniscus, blunting). Hypodense on CT.

blood.label: Blood / Hyperdense
blood.description: Hyperdense (white) on non-contrast CT. 50-70 HU acutely.

bone.label: Bone Disruption
bone.description: Cortical break, lucent line, step-off, angulation.

soft_tissue.label: Soft Tissue Changes
soft_tissue.description: Swelling, fat pad displacement, calcification, mass.

beforeYouSpeak.examinerTip: These 7 steps take 10-15 seconds when practised. They are worth 10-20% of the marks on most OSCE marking schemes. Students who skip them and jump to 'I can see a pneumothorax' lose easy marks — even if their diagnosis is correct.

steps.action: Check the image to ensure patient identity : check at least three patient identifies (example, patient name, date of birth, and hospital number)
steps.ifMissing: If no patient details visible: 'I note there are no patient identifiers on this image — in clinical practice I would confirm the patient identity before reporting.'
steps.label: Patient Identification
steps.say: 'I have confirmed patient identity and will now proceed reading the study.'
steps.why: Confirms you are interpreting the correct patient's image. In clinical practice, wrong-patient errors cause harm. Examiners mark this explicitly.

steps.action: Check the date/time stamp on the image.
steps.ifMissing: If no date: 'The date of this study is not visible — I would confirm when this was taken.'
steps.label: Date of Study
steps.why: Establishes whether the image is current or historical. A 3-week-old CXR may not reflect today's clinical status.

steps.action: Identify the view: PA vs AP, erect vs supine, lateral, axial, etc.
steps.label: View / Projection

modality_specifics.AXR: AP supine is standard. If erect: specifically look for air-fluid levels and free air under diaphragm.
modality_specifics.CT Brain: 'Axial non-contrast CT brain.' State window: 'on soft tissue windows' or 'on bone windows.'
modality_specifics.CXR: PA erect is standard. AP if portable/sick patient — state 'I note this is an AP film, so heart size assessment is limited.'
modality_specifics.MSK: Minimum 2 views at 90 degrees. State both: 'AP and lateral views of the [joint].' If only one view: 'I note only one view is available — I would request a second view at 90 degrees in most situations to allow optimum assessment.'

steps.say: 'This is a [PA erect / AP supine / lateral / axial non-contrast] [modality].'
steps.why: The view changes your interpretation: AP magnifies the heart (pseudocardiomegaly), supine films layer effusions posteriorly (invisible), rotation widens the mediastinum. Stating the view shows the examiner you understand these pitfalls.

steps.action: Confirm the L or R marker on the image. Check it correlates with the anatomy.
steps.label: Side Marker and Laterality
steps.say: 'The side marker indicates this is the [left/right] side. The marker correlates with the [anatomical landmark, e.g., gastric bubble on the left, heart apex on the left].'
steps.trap: A deliberately mislabelled image can be an OSCE trap. If the marker doesn't correlate: 'I note the side marker does not correlate with the anatomy — I would confirm laterality with the radiographer before reporting.'
steps.why: Wrong-side errors are a never event in clinical practice. Examiners specifically test whether students check laterality. On a CXR: gastric bubble should be under the LEFT hemidiaphragm. On MSK: the marker should match the side of the body.

steps.action: If age and sex are provided (on the image or in the clinical vignette), state them.
steps.label: Patient Demographics
steps.why: Age and sex change your differential. A 25-year-old with a lung mass → think lymphoma/germ cell. A 70-year-old → think primary lung cancer. A child with an elbow fracture → think supracondylar. Stating demographics shows you're thinking about pre-test probability.

steps.action: Assess whether the image is of diagnostic quality before interpreting it.

AXR: Coverage: from diaphragm to pubic symphysis included?
Exposure: can you see the psoas lines and renal outlines?
CT Brain: Windows: are both soft tissue and bone windows available?
Motion artefact: is the image degraded by patient movement?
CXR: Rotation: are the medial ends of the clavicles equidistant from the spinous processes?
Inspiration: can you count 5-7 anterior ribs above the diaphragm?
Exposure/Penetration: can you just see the vertebral bodies through the cardiac shadow?
Coverage: are the lung apices and both costophrenic angles included?
MSK: Two views: are AP and lateral both available?
Coverage: does the image include the joint above and below the injury?
Exposure: can you see cortical bone and soft tissues?

steps.ifSuboptimal: 'This image is [rotated/underexposed/poorly inspired]. If needed, I will consider requesting a repeat study, but I will interpret with this limitation in mind.'
steps.label: Technical Quality (Adequacy)
steps.say: 'The image is of [adequate/suboptimal] quality. [If suboptimal: specify the issue].'
steps.why: A rotated CXR can fake a widened mediastinum. Poor inspiration can fake cardiomegaly. If the image is suboptimal, state it — examiners want to hear you recognise limitations. If adequate, say so briefly and move on.

steps.action: Read the clinical information / referral question if provided.
steps.ifNone: If no clinical context: 'No clinical information is provided — I will perform a systematic review.'
steps.label: Clinical Context
steps.say: 'The clinical indication is [chest pain / fall / shortness of breath / trauma].'
steps.why: The clinical context directs your search pattern. 'Trauma' means look for fractures, pneumothorax, haemothorax. 'SOB' means look for consolidation, effusion, pulmonary oedema. Stating the context shows you are goal-directed, not just pattern-matching blindly.

beforeYouSpeak.subtitle: These are free marks. Every OSCE marking scheme scores them. Never skip them.
beforeYouSpeak.title: Before You Speak — The First 15 Seconds

Common Mistakes.fix: Always start with the 7 identification steps. 'I can see a pneumothorax' without stating the view, side marker, or quality loses easy marks.
Complete EVERY step of ABCDE/ABCS. The examiner may have placed a second finding you'll miss if you stop after the first.
Common Mistakes.mistake: Skipping the systematic approach after spotting the obvious finding

Common Mistakes.fix: Radiology provides differentials, not diagnoses. Say 'consistent with' or 'in keeping with'.
Common Mistakes.mistake: Saying 'this IS pneumonia' instead of 'consistent with'

Common Mistakes.fix: A rotated CXR can fake a widened mediastinum. State the quality — even 'adequate' shows you've checked.
If it's an emergency, SAY it's an emergency. 'This requires urgent [intervention]' — examiners mark this explicitly.
Common Mistakes.mistake: Forgetting to state urgency for emergencies

Common Mistakes.fix: Always have 2-3 differentials ready. Single-diagnosis answers suggest you haven't considered alternatives.

commonQuestions.question: What is the differential diagnosis?
commonQuestions.tip: Give 2-3 differentials, most likely first. For each: state one distinguishing feature. Example: 'The main differential is lobar pneumonia, but I would also consider pulmonary infarction — the absence of air bronchograms might favour infarction.'

commonQuestions.question: What investigation would you do next?
commonQuestions.tip: Be SPECIFIC. 'CT pulmonary angiogram with IV contrast' not just 'CT'. For trauma: 'trauma CT with IV contrast (CT head, C-spine, chest, abdomen, pelvis)'. For stroke: 'urgent CT brain followed by CT angiography if within treatment window.'

commonQuestions.question: How would you manage this patient?
commonQuestions.tip: Structure as: 1) A-E assessment for emergencies, 2) specific intervention (chest drain, antibiotics, surgery referral), 3) monitoring. Don't just say 'refer to surgery' — state what you'd do while waiting.

commonQuestions.question: What is the mechanism of injury?
commonQuestions.tip: Link mechanism to injury pattern: fall on outstretched hand → scaphoid/distal radius. Dashboard injury → posterior hip dislocation/femoral shaft. Deceleration → aortic injury. Fall from height → calcaneal fracture + lumbar spine.

commonQuestions.question: Is this normal or abnormal?
commonQuestions.tip: If normal: demonstrate your FULL systematic approach — this is what they're testing. If abnormal: state the abnormality, then complete the systematic review. Never say 'it looks normal' without proving you've checked everything.

commonQuestions.question: What are the complications of this condition?
commonQuestions.tip: Think: immediate (death, organ damage), early (infection, compartment syndrome), late (malunion, avascular necrosis, post-traumatic arthritis). Be specific to the diagnosis.

commonQuestions.question: What would you tell the patient?
commonQuestions.tip: Simple language: 'The X-ray shows a broken bone in your [location]. You will need [treatment]. Recovery takes approximately [timeframe].' Show empathy and avoid jargon.

commonQuestions.question: What if you don't know the diagnosis?
commonQuestions.tip: DON'T PANIC. State: 'I am not certain of the diagnosis, but the main findings are [describe what you see]. The differential includes [2-3 options]. I would recommend [next investigation] to clarify.' A structured uncertainty scores higher than a confident wrong answer.

keyPhrases.marks: Shows you recognise the urgency — high-scoring phrase when appropriate
keyPhrases.when: Tension pneumothorax, bowel perforation, bowel obstruction with ischaemia, epidural haematoma with midline shift

keyPhrases.marks: Shows you know the next step in the investigation pathway
keyPhrases.when: Widened mediastinum (aortic dissection), new focal neurology, suspected vascular injury, equivocal fracture

keyPhrases.marks: Demonstrates radiological caution. Radiology provides a differential, not a definitive diagnosis.
keyPhrases.when: ALWAYS — never say 'this IS X', say 'consistent with X'

keyPhrases.marks: Appropriate when findings need clinical context to interpret
keyPhrases.when: Subtle findings, incidental findings, findings that could be chronic or acute

keyPhrases.marks: Shows you think about temporal progression, not just one snapshot
keyPhrases.phrase: I would like to compare with previous imaging
keyPhrases.when: Chronic conditions, progressive disease, post-operative changes, follow-up studies

keyPhrases.marks: Demonstrates safety awareness — you've looked for the dangerous diagnosis and excluded it
keyPhrases.phrase: There are no features of [important negative]
keyPhrases.when: Trauma: 'no pneumothorax'. SOB: 'no pulmonary oedema'. Head injury: 'no intracranial haemorrhage'

keyPhrases.marks: Links imaging to clinical reasoning — shows you're not just a pattern-matcher
keyPhrases.phrase: I would take a focused history to clarify...
keyPhrases.when: When imaging findings could be explained by multiple clinical scenarios

keyPhrases.marks: Giving a sensible differential with reasoning scores higher than a confident wrong answer
keyPhrases.phrase: The main differential includes X, Y, and Z
keyPhrases.when: When you're not 100% sure of the diagnosis — this is better than guessing

sections.notes: Cover all 7 'Before You Speak' steps in 2-3 sentences. This takes 10-15 seconds.
sections.template: 'This is a [PA erect / AP supine / axial non-contrast] [modality] of [patient name/age/sex if given], taken on [date]. The side marker is [confirmed/not visible]. The image is of [adequate/suboptimal] quality. The clinical indication is [reason].'

sections.notes: Say what jumps out. If nothing jumps out, say so — it shows confidence, not ignorance. Then proceed systematically.
sections.template: 'On initial inspection, [the most obvious abnormality is... / there is no immediately obvious abnormality — I will proceed with a systematic review].'

sections.notes: Walk through EVERY step. For normal findings, say 'A — Airway: trachea midline, no abnormality.' Don't skip steps just because you've already spotted the diagnosis.
sections.template: 'Using the [ABCDE / ABCS / BBCB] approach: [A — ..., B — ..., C — ..., etc.]'

sections.notes: Say 'consistent with', never 'this IS'. If uncertain: 'The main differential includes X and Y. I would recommend Z to distinguish between them.'
sections.template: 'In summary, the key findings are [list 1-3 findings]. These are consistent with a diagnosis of [diagnosis].'

sections.notes: Emergencies: state urgency explicitly. Non-emergencies: suggest next investigation or management. Always end with a recommendation.
sections.template: '[If emergency:] This is a [surgical/medical] emergency requiring [action]. [If non-urgent:] I would recommend [next step / clinical correlation / follow-up].'

breakdown.description: Patient ID, date, view, side marker, quality, clinical context (the 7 steps above)
Walk through the modality-specific approach (ABCDE / ABCS / BBCB). Note ALL findings — normal and abnormal.
Structured presentation: identify → findings → diagnosis → urgency → recommendation
Examiner follow-up: differentials, management, next investigation, complications
